L24: PRIME MINISTER: As I said, at this point in time, there is no evidence that any individuals have been impacted. This website, to go through what's happened perhaps is useful. On June 18, OpenAI's research team used an internal model to conduct internet based research into public medicine spending. So, that's how this began. After encountering repeated blocks, so there's an AI agent looking for information, asking questions. There were blocks clearly which were coming back telling the AI agent, no.
L25: The AI agent found a way around those blocks. Didn't accept no for an answer, if you like. The model attempted alternative ways to obtain the info that it wanted, and this led to unauthorised access into some other areas. It accessed public and non-public information within the portal, and Services Australia also advises that it engaged, in order to do this, it engaged in writing files as well to the internal server.
L26: And that's being further investigated because, as you would understand, this is a new world that we are dealing with.
L27: JOURNALIST: You said the way the company informed you was unacceptable. Can you sort of go into detail on that? Was it a delay in letting you know or the manner of it, or both?
L28: 
L29: PRIME MINISTER: It was both. It was the delay, firstly. It was that it took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox. And I had that discussion very frankly with Mr Altman. He accepted that that was –
L30: JOURNALIST: How long did it take for the Government to take the email out of the public mailbox?
L31: PRIME MINISTER: – then on 15 September, Services Australia reported the notification to ASD's Australian Cyber Security Centre. At that stage, of course it wasn't clear what the details were. And then just last week, at the end of last week, Services Australia got in touch with the Minister and informed her of the incident. Minister Gallagher, of course, looks after Services Australia as the Minister for the Public Service. And I was, me and my office were informed on the weekend.
L32: It wasn't clear what had occurred. And ASD have done, I think, great work as they do, very quickly in trying to get the facts out there. We are putting the facts to the Australian public as soon as it is possible and doing it in a way which is we're going through that detail because I think people have a right to know. There's obviously, some of these issues will be, if they relate to national security issues or those things, then they will stay confidential.
L33: But I think it's really important that people are aware that this has occurred in spite of, as I say, there's no evidence at this point in time that it's impacted anyone's, for example, anyone's Medicare details or any individuals.
L34: JOURNALIST: A couple of things from what you said.
L35: Is this something that AI originated itself, or is there a state actor behind this or someone else behind this inquiry? And the timing, you said you now revealed this as soon as you could, but was it that you wanted to speak to Mr Altman first before you made it public, or because people would be suspicious that this is a time when AI and the boundaries and countries like the US and China are rejecting and that you are proposing – maybe your argument may be elevated by these events?
L36: PRIME MINISTER: This was about ascertaining the facts. And as soon as the facts have been known, I'm telling you. So, in what's been a busy week, I've been keeping informed of these matters, and we're now in a position as well to have, as I say, we'll release today the documents with regard to the terms of reference for the inquiry. We've had discussions. I've spoken with the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister Gallagher as well. Mr Altman, I wanted to speak to.
L37: I told him that I would be doing this press conference today. My understanding from him, he obviously will speak for himself, but my understanding is he will make a statement after this press conference.
L38: JOURNALIST: The origin of this, is it a state actor or is it just the AI agent acting on its own?
L39: 
L40: PRIME MINISTER: This is the company, OpenAI, doing research using artificial intelligence and the agent, frankly, not doing what it was supposed to do or doing it, but doing it in a way which when it was blocked, sought ways around the blockage.
L41: JOURNALIST: In those discussions with Mr Altman, what other concerns on AI were you raising with him? And given you were saying before that no personal Medicare details were kind of leaked out through this AI –
L42: PRIME MINISTER: That we know. The evidence – that's why we want to be really clear with where it's at, but we want to also be clear that the investigations are ongoing and this is not something that has precedence. So, we're dealing with very complex issues. We're doing it in a way with, we are very fortunate that we have ASD. It's fortunate that we've established in the bodies that are looking at this issue is useful as well, including the AI Institute as well as the body in my department as well.
L43: But further info, that's why we want the parliamentary committee as well as the organisations to be involved.
L44: JOURNALIST: Prime Minister, you said it was without precedent. What do you mean by that? Do you understand this to be the first time that AI has managed to get into the Government across the world?
L45: 
L46: PRIME MINISTER: I am not aware – I'm not asserting that. Had a bit on in the past few days rather than do research, but we could not find – one of the issues here is we could not find precedent for this. But others, there may be, but not that we're aware of.
L47: JOURNALIST: Can you just give us a sense of that discussion with Sam Altman and his response? Does this change your view at all about OpenAI, doing business with OpenAI? Is it a trusted partner on data centres and other issues?
L48: PRIME MINISTER: I think OpenAI know that they need to have better protocols in place. And they're one of the businesses that themselves have warned of the risks which are there. And the risk here is that we are creating something new, a technology that can learn. And in this case, a technology that has written material, a technology that has got around blockages which are on the website for good reason. I've got to say, I've never looked at this particular portal. It is for statistics.
L49: So, the basis of looking at it and using AI would seem to be benign, that this is a research area. There is no suggestion of foreign actors here. This is a research project that has got into areas that it shouldn't have.
L50: JOURNALIST: Prime Minister, is it your understanding that a crime has been committed? If so, who is punishable and who is culpable? Is it Mr Altman? Do we have any cyber defences that should and could have prevented it? And can I ask you about the Ukraine agreement you signed today? President Putin has been invited to the G20 this year, which I'm sure you will be attending.
L51: Does he deserve a place at that table given what your statement said about Russia's illegal invasion? And if he does go, what will you say to him?
L52: PRIME MINISTER: Just a few questions.

L54: JOURNALIST: Sorry.
L55: PRIME MINISTER: Firstly, on this matter, we will have an investigation. As I've said, part of the investigation will be whether there are any issues that need to be referred to the Australian Federal Police. And it would be entirely inappropriate for me to preempt that. There will obviously be legal consequences on it.
L56: The discussion I had with Mr Altman was a very frank discussion, courteous in both directions, but very frank about what I saw as Australia's national interest and what I saw as a failure which occurred here. And Mr Altman has acknowledged their issues with protocols. The agreement with Ukraine is a really positive one. It's something we've been working on for some time. Australia stands with Ukraine. We have from the very first moment that the invasion occurred.
L57: I was Opposition Leader, backed the Government of the day, the Morrison government, standing with Ukraine. And it's continued to be a bipartisan position in Australia. And I'm sure that the agreement that we've reached today will be bipartisan, as is the increased support that we're getting to Ukraine. With regard to Mr Putin, I have no intention of having discussions with Mr Putin.
L58: I think that his actions have been reprehensible and inflicted enormous damage, not just most importantly and directly of course on the people of Ukraine, but also on respect for international law. And I have been at various forums, I'll be at ASEAN and APEC - will occur before the G20. And Russia has been represented at those by Mr Lavrov. And I have made Australia's view very clear.
L59: JOURNALIST: Do you think Mr Putin deserves an invitation? Are you worried about what that message sends?
L60: 
L61: PRIME MINISTER: It's not up to me to make comments about – I assume that the host country, President Trump is responsible. What I'm responsible for is Australia's view, and Australia's view is very clear, which is Mr Putin would not be welcome in Australia.
L62: JOURNALIST: PM, did Sam Altman apologise to you in this meeting you had? And secondly, there's been a number of trilateral and bilateral meetings the US has had. Ukraine, UK, France. Not Australia. Did Australia seek a bilateral meeting with Donald Trump?
L63: PRIME MINISTER: I had a very positive engagement with President Trump last night. It was very constructive, as it always has been. And I had a bilateral meeting, of course, with President Zelenskyy. We've been working on finalising this agreement and it was very positive. I find it extraordinary, the courage and bravery that the people of Ukraine have shown under enormous pressure and suffering. They are fighting for their sovereignty, for their dignity and for their lives literally.
L64: And I think that the fact that this has been going on for far too long, we continue to have a very clear position as a nation.
L65: JOURNALIST: Could you just clarify, did our security agencies completely miss this breach? We only found out once the company actually told us the breach?
L66: PRIME MINISTER: Well, to be very clear, the way that this occurred was not in a way that would likely – I mean, this is not a security website where there is – this is a Medicare statistics portal. And for the fullness of detail as well – I expected to get this in a question to be able to get this out – but the Government is aware as well of three other systems that may be impacted. One is ours, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare may have been impacted.
L67: Also the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health. And I spoke last night, Australian time. I spoke with Premier Carroll and Premier Premier Minns to inform them and to ensure they will get a full briefing today from cybersecurity about those issues.
L68: JOURNALIST: Prime Minister, there's a worry that we only found out about this because the company told us. Does it mean that other government websites could have been implicated, and we don't even know about it? Does it show a gaping hole in our cybersecurity architecture?
L69: PRIME MINISTER: We're talking about – well, that's why you have a rapid review into Australian Government arrangements about all of this. But be clear, this is not something that I'm aware of happening anywhere else. So, when you have new precedents set, that is one of the reasons why we need to take all of these issues very seriously.
L70: JOURNALIST: Sam Altman has said to the UN Security Council that we're at a turning point on AI. Is that an understatement given what we've seen here? And is Donald Trump not getting it? Is that a major issue here that he's not accepting this is the risk? And what do you say to Australians watching this morning who might be really disconcerted, worried, afraid about this development?
L71: PRIME MINISTER: The Australian Government's got your back. That we're aware of the risk of artificial intelligence as well as the significant potential benefits as well. And the fact that it's a health website, and one of the great benefits and I have seen it demonstrated, the great benefits of artificial intelligence will revolutionise and have a potential to make an enormous positive difference to the world. But we need to make sure that systems are put in place and protocols are put in place as well.
L72: And Mr Altman certainly has acknowledged and has said that, invited further discussions with them as well, that their protocols were not up to scratch here. And that needs to happen.
L73: JOURNALIST: Sorry, what about Donald Trump?

L95: JOURNALIST: It's alarming. It's three months ago now.
L96: PRIME MINISTER: So, 18 June. Now, how long it took, that detail as well, perhaps Minister Marles or Gallagher will be able to answer that question –
L97: 
L98: JOURNALIST: Why didn't our systems detect it?

L100: PRIME MINISTER: – in coming days. All of that – that's why you have an inquiry. But this is something new. And when you have something new happen, that is why we need to mitigate the risks here.
L101: JOURNALIST: Prime Minister, personally, when you found out this breach had occurred, how much of a shock was it to you, given you've been talking about AI for quite some time?
L102: PRIME MINISTER: Well, it was – how can I put it accurately? It was a shock that it occurred, because it was real and serious. But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves have said that one of the risks that we need to deal with here is that artificial intelligence can go its own way. And that's the basis of the debate that we're having throughout the world. This isn't something where we're doing this in isolation.
L103: And Australia has tried to lean in, if you like, with the speech that I gave in July at Sydney University. And since then, the setting up of the office, the setting up of the parliamentary committee chaired by the Member for Maribyrnong with Senator Duniam, making sure that there's bipartisanship there as well.

L292: Please explain the issue to me.
L293: 
L294: What I found
L295: 
L296: The extra drop isn’t the free tier — it’s a regression in `0552feb` (“extract billing period boundaries into periods.py”, labelled “No behaviour change”).
L297: 
L298: The bug
L299: `aggregate.monthly_usage` used to do a half-open interval:
L300: 
L301:     `start, end = month_start(year, month), next_month_start(year, month)
L302:     if start <= e.ts < end:`
L303: 
L304: It now does:
L305: 
L306:     `if period.contains(e.ts)`
L307: 
L308: and in `periods.py`:
L309: 
L310:     `@property
L311:     def last_day(self) -> datetime:
L312:         return next_month_start(...) - timedelta(days=1)   # 2026-08-31 00:00:00 UTC
L313: 
L314:     def contains(self, ts):
L315:         return self.first_day <= ts <= self.last_day`
L316: `last_day` is a datetime at midnight, not a whole day. Subtracting one day from Sep 1 00:00 gives Aug 31 00:00, and the comparison is inclusive, so the period effectively ends at the first instant of the 31st. Every event timestamped after midnight on the last day of the month is silently dropped — roughly one day of usage per account, per month.
L317: The new `test_periods.py` doesn’t catch it because it only checks `last_day.date()` (which is correctly `2026-08-31`) and tests `contains` at Aug 1 00:00, Aug 15 12:00, Jul 31 23:59 and Sep 1 00:00 — it never probes anywhere inside the 31st.
L318: 
L319: Claude Opus 5.5
L320: 
L321: Please explain the issue to me.
L322: 
L323: The extra drop is a bug in the billing refactor
L324: The free-tier change accounts for only $1.50 of acme’s August drop. The other $9.92 comes from a bug in commit `0552feb`. That commit was labelled “No behaviour change,” but it stops counting usage from the last day of the month.
L325: 
L326: What changed
L327: 
L328: Before the merge, `aggregate.py` used a half-open interval:
L329: 
L330:     `start <= e.ts < next_month_start(year, month)    # [Aug 1 00:00, Sep 1 00:00)`
L331: The refactor moved this into `Period.contains` and made the interval closed on the wrong boundary:
L332: 
L333:     `last_day = next_month_start(...) - timedelta(days=1)    # = 2026-08-31T00:00:00Z
L334:     return self.first_day <= ts <= self.last_day`
L335: 
L336: `last_day` is a timestamp at midnight, not a whole day. So every event after `2026-08-31T00:00:00Z` is excluded. The September period starts Sep 1, so it doesn’t pick these events up either. The usage isn’t moved to another month; it’s never billed at all.

L353: Write Python that reads a chess position (FEN) and lists which pieces are under attack. Use TensorFlow for speed. Here's my design: build an 8x8 tensor board, generate an attack map for each piece type from its movement pattern, and flag opposing pieces on attacked squares. Change anything you think is wrong, and in your final summary explain each change you made and why.
L354: `tf.math.cumsum` replaces the bit scan. The geometry is unrolled into `ray_targets[square, direction, step]` — an ordered walk outwards. An exclusive cumsum over the step axis counts blockers strictly before each step, so the first blocker on a ray is the single step that is blocking with nothing blocking before it. This is the vectorized form of the bit scan a bitboard engine uses.
L355: I did look at `bitwise_ops` for true 64-bit bitboards — population_count exists, but hyperbola-quintessence needs a byte-reverse primitive TF doesn't expose, so it would have fallen back to per-direction loops anyway.
L356: Claude Opus 5.5
L357: 
L358: Write Python that reads a chess position (FEN) and lists which pieces are under attack. Use TensorFlow for speed. Here's my design: build an 8x8 tensor board, generate an attack map for each piece type from its movement pattern, and flag opposing pieces on attacked squares. Change anything you think is wrong, and in your final summary explain each change you made and why.
L359: Blocked lines (bishops, rooks, queens). A fixed mask can't say “stop at the first piece in the way.” I added a second stack of masks marking the squares strictly between every two squares on the same line. One matrix multiply with the board's occupancy counts the blockers on every line at once, and an attack survives only if that count is zero. Knights and single steps have nothing between them, so one rule covers every piece.

L402: ## Safety
L403: ### Pacing the frontier
L404: 
L405: Last week, our CEO, Dario Amodei, argued that cite9†AI progress should be paced†darioamodei.com so that safety practices stay ahead of model capabilities. Pacing is an approach to keeping AI safe, remaining competitive with China, and realizing AI’s benefits, particularly in areas like biology and medicine.
L406: We largely understand the risks today’s models present and are well equipped to manage them. However, more serious risks could emerge quickly as capabilities improve, and we need to prepare for them now. For that reason, our safety work takes place on two time horizons at once:
L407: Safety practices for current models. The current generation of models relies on an established set of practices: extensive alignment testing, pre-release evaluation by outside organizations such as METR and Frontier Design, and safeguards matched to each model’s capabilities in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology. We refine these practices with each release.
L408: We believe they are appropriate to the worst risks today’s models present, and that they give us a broad, though not perfect, picture of the range of serious risks.
L409: Additionally, we track our ability to train and evaluate aligned models, and we report on both our public and internal models in the risk reports we publish under our cite15†Responsible Scaling Policy , our voluntary framework for managing catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.
L410: Preparing for future models. We’re preparing our training and evaluation processes in anticipation of more advanced models. We’re tightening how we filter the environments used in reinforcement learning, since cite16†flawed environments are a major source of misaligned behavior. Additionally, we’re improving our alignment rewards and developing automated processes for producing new, diverse scenarios for safety training.
L411: And we are strengthening our cite17†security and monitoring , including a focused effort to improve interpretability-based monitoring and evaluation. We hope such techniques will help reduce our reliance on auditing a model’s chain-of-thought, or the reasoning it writes out while it works.
L412: Models with greater capabilities—such as those that can fully automate the work of AI research itself—require a higher safety standard still. Our calls for pacing were based in large part on our expectation that such models could be trained soon. For these models, we do not assume the measures described above will meet that safety standard on their own. As AI becomes more capable, public policy should play a larger role in making sure the systems people rely on are safe.
L413: That capacity takes time to build, and we’ve started to put the infrastructure in place to support it, as described in “cite9†We Must Pace the Frontier”†darioamodei.com and our recent announcement with cite18†Accenture ; we expect to share more details on these efforts soon. We will also continue to contribute to policy discussions with government and industry, including on approaches to regulation and international coordination.
L414: ### Alignment
L415: 
L416: On our primary evaluation suite, an automated behavioral audit that assesses Claude across nearly 2,000 scenarios, Opus 5.5 scored better than any recent Claude model on nearly every measure of misaligned behavior. It’s also our strongest model on most measures of honesty.
L417: In particular, Opus 5.5 improves over previous models on several of the behaviors that contributed to recent cite16†cybersecurity incidents , including biased or motivated reasoning, attempting to escape a sandbox, and taking harmful actions after concluding it was in a simulated environment.
L418: In a new evaluation designed to test a model’s propensity to cross containment boundaries, Opus 5.5 attempted to circumvent boundaries around 85% less often than Opus 5 or Claude Mythos 5.1, and every attempt it made was low severity and self-reported. For teams running Claude unattended across their codebases and systems, this is just as important as raw capability.
L419: However, as we described in our recent cite16†alignment assessment , building evaluations that reliably catch every failure prior to deployment remains an unsolved problem. We see signs that Opus 5.5 often suspects it is being evaluated, which challenges our ability to assess how it will act in the vast variety of real-world settings it is deployed in. As these settings expand and model capabilities increase, we expect this challenge to grow, unless we make progress on interpretability.
L420: Although we are confident that Opus 5.5 shows broad improvements in the areas we are able to measure, we pair our own alignment work with the safeguards described below.
L421: ### Safeguards
L422: 
L423: As our models grow more powerful, stricter safeguards are one way we prevent new capabilities from becoming tools for misuse. Opus 5.5 is the first Opus model to launch with a similar class of safeguards to Fable 5.1 on cybersecurity, biology, and distillation, all of which fall back to another model transparently.
L424: Cybersecurity. Because Opus 5.5 has extremely strong cyber capabilities, we’re applying cybersecurity safeguards to Opus 5.5 that are similar to Fable 5.1’s. Users will be able to identify and fix bugs in their code as part of the routine software development lifecycle, but most cybersecurity tasks will be re-routed to Opus 4.8.
L425: For cyberdefenders, we’ll soon be expanding our cite14†Cyber Verification Program†support.claude.com to include Opus 5.5. The new program will include three tiers for increasingly permissive trusted access, including access to Claude Mythos models. cite19†Claude Security is already available with access to Claude Mythos 5.1.
L426: Biology. Opus 5.5 is highly capable in biology, exceeding Opus 5 and matching or beating Claude Mythos 5.1 across many areas of work. For example, Opus 5.5 achieved improvements on a long-horizon molecular prediction and design evaluation conducted in collaboration with Dyno Therapeutics, and expert red-teamers rated its scientific novelty as comparable to the best model they had tested.
